Autoresearch

You already run Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse. Point one of them at a goal and it becomes a relentless improvement engine.

The idea is Karpathy's autoresearch: set a constraint, pick a mechanical metric, let the agent iterate on its own. The gains compound.

"Set the GOAL → The agent runs the LOOP → You wake up to results"

You don't need AGI. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that never quits.

Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse all work for the core skill, the bundled runtime, installation, and verification. Hook guardrails ship for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

Then there's fork-and-flush. Metric loops hit plateaus, so the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, the way Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447) do. This happens at 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep. Each branch runs briefly; the winner stays. Half the branches pick their own ideas (randomness). The other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Guided: R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it answers with FORK before it gives up. Details in guide/autoresearch.md.

bumblebee

Bumblebee is a read-only inventory collector for package, extension, and developer-tool metadata on macOS and Linux developer endpoints.

It answers one narrow supply-chain response question: an advisory names a package, extension, or version, and you need to know which developer machines show a match in their on-disk metadata right now.

SBOMs tell you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Supply-chain response often needs a messier view: local state across lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee turns that scattered on-disk state into structured NDJSON component records. Hand it an exposure catalog and it flags exact matches, so you can run fast, read-only exposure checks when you already know what you're looking for.

SkillsBench tests whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across diverse domains. It measures how much a model's ability to solve complex real-world tasks improves when it has specialized Skills.

But in production, you don't get one Skill per task. You get hundreds installed at once. So we adapted SkillsBench to match that reality. In the original setup, each task comes with only its own specialized Skill. In our version, every task runs in a global environment containing all 195 specialized Skills, and everything else stays the same. The question is simple: can an agent find the right Skills in a large installed pool, pick them itself, and arrange them into a workflow that actually completes the task?

We ran vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench, using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Against the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points, cut token consumption by 29.6%, and cut tool calls by 33.1%.

Semantic version control built on Git.

Git tells you lines changed. sem tells you what changed: functions, methods, classes.

Releases

sem is a semantic version control tool that runs on top of Git. It parses your code with tree-sitter, pulls out every function, class, and method as an entity, and diffs entities instead of lines. So instead of lines x-y changed, you read function blahh was modified.

Drop it into any Git repo. No setup.

Cloud-backed queries are opt-in per repo: logging in does not upload a repo or send a query. See the cloud consent flow for the public/private repo states, preview screen, local audit log, and forget controls.
